title: Word building
intro: Turkish makes new words by adding suffixes to old ones, and you have met many already: *Kanadalı*, *sessiz*, *aşçı*, *gözlük*, *Türkçe*. This unit names six of the most useful word-building suffixes (*yapım ekleri*): `-lI` (with, from), `-sIz` (without), `-CI` (the person who makes, sells or does), `-lIk` (-ness, a thing for, lasting), `-CA` (languages, manner, opinion) and the distributive `-(ş)Ar` (each), with `-leyin` for times of day. Each makes a new word, which then takes the usual endings: *gözlüğüm*, *gazeteciler*, *Türkçeyi*.

blocks.text: `-lI` turns a noun into an adjective meaning **with, having, containing**. It follows four-way harmony, and its l never changes: *şekerli* (with sugar, sweetened), *sütlü* (with milk), *tuzlu* (salty), *bulutlu* (cloudy), *akıllı* (clever: with brains).

On a place name, `-lI` means **from**: *İstanbullu* (from Istanbul), *Ankaralı*, *İzmirli*, and the *Kanadalı* of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03). It makes a new word, so there is no apostrophe: *İstanbullu*, not *İstanbul'lu*. *Nereli?* asks **from where?**: *Nerelisin? — İzmirliyim.*

head: Noun
+ -lI
Meaning
rows: from Istanbul; a person from Istanbul

blocks.text: Like any adjective, a word in `-lI` goes before its noun: *sütlü kahve* (coffee with milk), *bahçeli bir ev* (a house with a garden), *iki çocuklu bir aile* (a family with two children). It can also be the predicate: *Bugün hava bulutlu*. Some old ones have their own meaning: *tatlı* (sweet), *ünlü* (famous: with fame), *evli* (married).

items.en: Do you take your tea with sugar?
A coffee with milk, please.
This soup is very salty.
We're looking for a house with a garden.
I'm from Istanbul; my husband is from Ankara.

blocks.text: *Şekerli* and *şekerle* are not the same. *Şekerli çay* is a kind of tea, sweetened: `-lI` describes the noun. *Şekerle*, the `-(y)lA` of [A1 unit 12](gp-ile), says what you use: *Çayı şekerle içiyorum* (I drink my tea with sugar). Before a noun, only `-lI` works: *şekerli bir çay*.
`-lI` also names supporters of a club: *Galatasaraylı*, *Fenerbahçeli*, *Beşiktaşlı*. *Hangi takımlısın?* asks which team you support.

`-sIz` is the opposite of `-lI`: **without, -less**. It follows four-way harmony, and its s never changes: *şekersiz* (without sugar), *sütsüz* (without milk), *tuzsuz* (unsalted), *susuz* (without water), *işsiz* (unemployed: without work), *parasız* (free of charge; broke), and the *sessiz* (quiet: without sound) of [A1 unit 12](a1-u12).

Words in `-sIz` work as adjectives (*şekersiz bir kahve*), as predicates with the personal endings (*Kardeşim işsiz*, *Bugün parasızım*: I'm broke today) and sometimes as adverbs: *Çocuklar müzeye parasız giriyor* (Children get into the museum for free).

items.en: A tea without sugar, please.
My brother has been out of work for two months.
We can't live without water.
The museums are free today.
I drink my coffee without milk.

blocks.text: For a Turkish coffee, **without sugar** is *sade* (plain), as the [A1 interlude](a1-u12-culture) explains; *şekersiz* is for tea and other coffees.
`-sIz` is a word-building suffix, not the negative of a verb. **I don't take sugar** is *Şeker almıyorum*; *şekersiz* describes the drink.

`-CI` names the person who makes, sells, repairs or does something, and often the shop as well: *gazeteci* (journalist), *kitapçı* (bookseller; bookshop), *çiçekçi* (florist), *futbolcu* (footballer). It follows four-way harmony, and its C is c after a vowel or a voiced consonant, ç after a voiceless one (f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p), the same rule as the d and t of [A1 unit 5](gp-consonant-assimilation).

blocks.label: -CI
lines: -çı, -çi, -çu, -çü   after f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p

head: Noun
+ -CI
Meaning
rows: coffee maker or seller; coffee shop

blocks.text: The stem never softens before `-CI`, which starts with a consonant: *kitapçı*, *çiçekçi*, not *kitabçı*. The shop and the person share the word: *Kitapçıya gidiyorum* (I'm going to the bookshop). You know *aşçı* (cook) and *kapıcı* (caretaker) already; *kuyumcu* (jeweller) and *halıcı* (carpet seller) appear in the [interlude](a2-u12-culture), where whole streets are named with `-CI` in the plural.
Some `-CI` words describe a habit rather than a trade: *yalancı* (liar), *şakacı* (joker, someone who likes to joke).

items.en: My older sister is a journalist.
The bookshop is opposite the post office.
I bought some lovely flowers at the florist's.
Fishermen go out to sea early in the morning.
The passengers got on the bus.

blocks.text: `-CI` is close to English **-er** (baker) and French **-ier** (boulanger), but it names the shop too: *kitapçı* is the bookseller and the bookshop, as French libraire and librairie are almost one word.
`-lIk` follows four-way harmony and has three jobs.

items: **Abstract nouns**, like English **-ness, -hood, -ship**: *güzellik* (beauty), *iyilik* (goodness, a kindness), *gençlik* (youth), *arkadaşlık* (friendship), *hastalık* (illness), and the *çocukluk* (childhood) of [unit 2](a2-u02).
**A thing for something**: *gözlük* (glasses: for the eyes), *sözlük* (dictionary: for words), *kitaplık* (bookcase), *tuzluk* (salt shaker), *kulaklık* (headphones: for the ears).

**After a number and a measure**, an adjective of duration, size or value: *bir haftalık tatil* (a week's holiday), *iki saatlik yol* (a two-hour journey), *dört kişilik masa* (a table for four), *elli liralık bilet* (a fifty-lira ticket).

blocks.text: Its k softens to ğ before a vowel, like the k of most longer words ([A1 unit 8](gp-consonant-softening)): *gözlüğüm* (my glasses), *güzelliği* (its beauty), *kitaplığa* (to the bookcase). And the suffixes stack: *işsizlik* (unemployment: the state of being without work).

items.en: I can't find my glasses.
We're going on a week's holiday.
A table for four, please.
The books are in the bookcase.
I won't forget this kindness.

blocks.text: *Bir haftalık* describes a noun: *bir haftalık tatil*. After a verb, **for a week** is just *bir hafta*: *Bir hafta kaldık* (We stayed for a week).
*Ne var ne yok?* (What's new?) is often answered *İyilik, sağlık* (All is well: goodness, health).
`-CA` follows two-way harmony (*-ca, -ce*), and its C becomes ç after a voiceless consonant (*-ça, -çe*). It has three everyday jobs.

head: Use
Word
+ -CA
Meaning
rows: in your opinion; what do you think?

blocks.text: **Languages** are the people + `-CA`: *Türkçe, İngilizce, Fransızca, Almanca, İspanyolca, Rusça, Arapça, Japonca*. They take endings with no apostrophe: *Türkçeyi*, *İngilizcede* (in English).

**Manner.** On an adjective, `-CA` makes an adverb with a touch of care: *yavaşça* (slowly, gently), *sessizce* (quietly), *iyice* (thoroughly). The bare adjective of [unit 8](gp-adjectives-as-adverbs) is the everyday choice (*yavaş konuş*); `-CA` adds softness or care.

**Opinion.** On a pronoun, `-CA` means **in … opinion**: *bence* (in my opinion), *sence* (in your opinion), *bizce*, *sizce*. Alone, *Sence?* and *Sizce?* ask **What do you think?** *Bence* is the everyday twin of the *bana göre* of [unit 9](gp-postp-dative).

items.en: In my opinion this film is very good.
Which one do you think is better?
She closed the door gently.
My friend speaks Russian and Japanese.
I waited for you for hours!

blocks.text: On a plural number or time word, `-CA` means **by the …**: *yüzlerce* (hundreds of), *binlerce* (thousands of), *saatlerce* (for hours), *yıllarca* (for years).
Language names take their endings without an apostrophe: *Türkçede*, *İngilizceyi*, never *Türkçe'de*. They keep the capital of the people's name: *Türkçe*, *İngilizce*.

sections.title: Birer, ikişer; sabahleyin: each, and times of day

blocks.text: On a number, `-(ş)Ar` means **each, apiece**: *Çocuklara birer elma verdim* (I gave the children an apple each). It follows two-way harmony and takes ş after a vowel: *ikişer, altışar, yedişer*. The t of *dört* softens: *dörder*.

Doubled, they mean **in groups of**: *birer birer* (one by one), *ikişer ikişer* (two by two). *Kaçar?* asks **how many each?** or **how much each?**: *Biletler kaçar lira?* (How much is each ticket?)

**-leyin.** Four time words take `-leyin`, which never harmonizes: *sabahleyin* (in the morning), *öğleyin* (at noon, from *öğle*, noon), *akşamleyin* (in the evening), *geceleyin* (at night). They sound a little old-fashioned or written; speech also uses the bare words: *Sabah erken kalktım*.

items.en: I bought the children an ice cream each.
Everyone bought two books each.
The students came into the classroom one by one.
How much is each ticket?
I get up early in the morning.

blocks.text: *Birer* is not *bir*. *Çocuklara bir elma verdim* is one apple for all the children; *birer elma* is one apple each.
English needs **each** or **apiece** after the noun, and French chacun: they got two books each, ils ont eu deux livres chacun. Turkish marks the number: *ikişer kitap*.

summary: `-CI` names who makes, sells or does something, and often the shop: *gazeteci*, *kitapçı*; c after vowels and voiced consonants, ç after voiceless ones.
`-lIk` makes abstract nouns (*güzellik*), things for something (*gözlük*, *kitaplık*) and measures (*bir haftalık*, *dört kişilik*); its k softens: *gözlüğüm*.
`-CA` makes languages (*Türkçe*, *Rusça*), adverbs of manner (*yavaşça*) and opinions (*bence*, *sence*).
`-(ş)Ar` on a number means **each**: *birer*, *ikişer*, *dörder*; *birer birer* is **one by one**.
`-leyin` works on four time words only: *sabahleyin*, *öğleyin*, *akşamleyin*, *geceleyin*.
